```{r}
#| label: setup
source("functions.R")
pop <- populations$binomial
```

# 1. What population are you sampling from?

One draw from Binomial(5, 0.1) counts the successes in 5 independent trials when each trial succeeds with probability
0.1, for example the number of defective items in a box of 5 when each item is defective 10 percent of the time. It can
only be 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5. Its mean is 5 × 0.1 = 0.5 and its variance is 5 × 0.1 × 0.9 = 0.45 (SD about
`r round(pop$sigma, 3)`). It is right skewed (skewness (1 − 2p) / sqrt(5p(1 − p)) = `r round(pop$gamma1, 3)`) and its excess kurtosis is
(1 − 6p(1 − p)) / (5p(1 − p)) = `r round(pop$gamma2, 3)`.

All three CLT assumptions hold: the draws are independent, they all come from the same distribution, and the variance
is finite. So SE = sigma / sqrt(n) should apply.

This population combines the two problems I met before: it is skewed like the exponential (03exponential.qmd), and it
is discrete like the die (02die.qmd). It is also very lopsided: most draws are 0.

```{r}
#| label: population
#| fig.width: 7
#| fig.height: 4.5
set.seed(student_id)
popDraws <- pop$generator(100000)

trueProb <- dbinom(0:5, size = 5, prob = 0.1)
share <- as.numeric(table(factor(popDraws, levels = 0:5))) / length(popDraws)
plot(0:5, share, type = "h", lwd = 8, col = "gray60", ylim = c(0, 0.75), xlim = c(-2, 5.5),
     main = "Binomial(5, 0.1) population: 100,000 draws", xlab = "Value", ylab = "Proportion")
points(0:5, trueProb, pch = 4, cex = 1.5, lwd = 2, col = "firebrick")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = pop$mu, sd = pop$sigma), add = TRUE, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c("Simulated share", "True probability", "Normal with same mean and SD"),
       col = c("gray60", "firebrick", "steelblue"), lwd = c(8, 2, 2), lty = c(1, NA, 1), pch = c(NA, 4, NA), bty = "n")

data.frame(value = 0:5, trueProb = round(trueProb, 5), simulatedShare = share)

data.frame(
  quantity    = c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "excess kurtosis"),
  theoretical = c(pop$mu, pop$sigma, pop$gamma1, pop$gamma2),
  simulated   = c(mean(popDraws), sd(popDraws), skewness(popDraws), exKurtosis(popDraws))
)
```

`r round(100 * trueProb[1], 1)` percent of all draws are 0 and `r round(100 * trueProb[2], 1)` percent are 1; values of 4 or 5 are so rare
(`r round(100 * sum(trueProb[5:6]), 3)` percent together) that they hardly ever appear. The normal curve with the same mean and SD puts
`r round(100 * pnorm(-0.5, mean = pop$mu, sd = pop$sigma), 1)` percent of its area below −0.5, that is on negative counts, which are impossible.

To check that my 100,000 draws behave like this population, I ran a chi square test against the true probabilities.
The values 3, 4 and 5 are so rare that their expected counts are too small for the test (the expected count for 5 is
only `r round(100000 * trueProb[6], 1)`), so I combined them into one group "3 or more".

```{r}
#| label: populationCheck
observed <- c(table(factor(popDraws, levels = 0:5))[1:3], sum(popDraws >= 3))
names(observed) <- c("0", "1", "2", "3 or more")
expectedProb <- c(trueProb[1:3], sum(trueProb[4:6]))
popTest <- chisq.test(observed, p = expectedProb)
data.frame(group = names(observed), observed = as.numeric(observed), expected = round(100000 * expectedProb, 1))
popTest
```

The test did not reject the true probabilities (p = `r round(popTest$p.value, 3)`), so my draws are a typical sample from Binomial(5, 0.1).

# 2. What did you expect before running the simulation?

Binomial(5, 0.1) has both difficulties I met before at the same time: the discreteness of the die (02die.qmd) and the
skewness of the exponential (03exponential.qmd). I estimated how each of them affects the sampling distribution of the
mean, and predicted the smallest n that passes my standard from that.

## Center and spread

The CLT formulas for the mean and the standard error only need independent draws from the same distribution with a
finite variance, and this population meets all three. So I expected the mean of the sample means to be 0.5 and their
SD to be sigma / sqrt(n) = `r round(pop$sigma, 3)` / sqrt(n) at every n, even at n = 1.

## The n at which each check should pass

I used the formulas from my earlier files to find the n at which each check should reach my standard.

```{r}
#| label: prediction
skewN <- predictedN(pop$gamma1)
kurtN <- ceiling(pop$gamma2 / criteria$kurt)
dieStep <- 1 / (populations$die$sigma * sqrt(8))
gapN <- ceiling((1 / (pop$sigma * dieStep))^2)
c(skewN = skewN, kurtN = kurtN, gapN = gapN)
```

* Skewness: averaging shrinks it to gamma1 / sqrt(n). To meet my cutoff of `r criteria$skew` I need `r round(pop$gamma1, 3)` / sqrt(n) ≤ `r criteria$skew`, so
  n ≥ (`r round(pop$gamma1, 3)` / `r criteria$skew`)² ≈ `r skewN`.
* Kurtosis: it shrinks faster, like gamma2 / n. `r round(pop$gamma2, 3)` / n ≤ `r criteria$kurt` already holds from n = `r kurtN`.
* QQ correlation (the size of the gaps): the possible values of the mean are 1 / n apart, and for the gaps to disappear
  in the QQ plot they have to be small compared with the standard error. In SE units the gap is
  (1 / n) / (sigma / sqrt(n)) = 1 / (sigma × sqrt(n)) = 1 / (`r round(pop$sigma, 3)` × sqrt(n)). In 02die.qmd the QQ check passed when the gap was
  `r round(dieStep, 3)` SE (at n = 8). Using the same standard, 1 / (`r round(pop$sigma, 3)` × sqrt(n)) ≤ `r round(dieStep, 3)` gives n ≥ (1 / (`r round(pop$sigma, 3)` × `r round(dieStep, 3)`))² ≈ `r gapN`.

## My prediction and n = 30

The largest of the three, n = `r gapN`, should be the bottleneck, so I predicted that the gaps would decide the answer at
about n = `r gapN`.

I did not expect the rule of thumb n = 30 to be enough. At n = 30 the formula gives a skewness of
`r round(pop$gamma1 / sqrt(30), 3)`, above my cutoff of `r criteria$skew`, and a gap of `r round(1 / (pop$sigma * sqrt(30)), 3)` SE, larger than the `r round(dieStep, 3)` SE at which the die passed, so I
expected visible steps in the QQ plot.

## Tails at n = 1

At n = 1 the sample mean is a single draw. Even the smallest value, 0, is only `r round(0.5 / pop$sigma, 2)` SDs below the mean of 0.5, so
nothing can fall in the lower tail beyond −1.96 SDs. On the right, every value of 2 or more is in the upper tail,
`r round(100 * sum(trueProb[3:6]), 2)` percent of the draws. So I expected tail shares of 0 and about 8 percent at n = 1.

## Why my prediction might be wrong

If n = `r gapN` is wrong, I expected the true answer to be larger. The prediction borrows the QQ standard from the die, which
was symmetric. Binomial(5, 0.1) has steps and a strong right skew at the same time, so two things lower its QQ
correlation instead of one, and the gaps may have to become smaller than they did for the die before the QQ check
passes.

## The exact distribution

The sum of n independent Binomial(5, 0.1) draws is Binomial(5n, 0.1), so the exact distribution of the sample mean is
Binomial(5n, 0.1) / n. As in 02die.qmd, I used it to see what the formulas miss, without any simulation.

```{r}
#| label: exactBinom
exactBinomMean <- function(n) {
  data.frame(value = (0:(5 * n)) / n, prob = dbinom(0:(5 * n), size = 5 * n, prob = 0.1))
}
exactN <- c(1, 5, 10, 30, skewN, 50, 100)
exactTable <- do.call(rbind, lapply(exactN, function(n) {
  e <- exactBinomMean(n)
  d <- e$value - sum(e$value * e$prob)
  v <- sum(d^2 * e$prob)
  se <- pop$sigma / sqrt(n)
  data.frame(n = n,
             stepInSE = (1 / n) / se,
             formulaSkew = pop$gamma1 / sqrt(n),
             exactSkew = sum(d^3 * e$prob) / v^1.5,
             largestCdfGap = cdfGap(e$value, e$prob, pop$mu, se),
             withCorrection = cdfGap(e$value, e$prob, pop$mu, se, shift = 1 / (2 * n)))
}))
knitr::kable(exactTable, digits = 4)
```

The exact skewness equals the formula, so the formula is right about the skewness. `largestCdfGap` is the largest
vertical distance between the exact CDF of the mean and the normal CDF, and `withCorrection` is the same distance when
the normal CDF is evaluated half a step to the right (a continuity correction). At n = 30 the normal approximation can
be off by `r round(100 * exactTable$largestCdfGap[exactTable$n == 30], 1)` percentage points without the correction and `r round(100 * exactTable$withCorrection[exactTable$n == 30], 1)` with it. For the die at n = 8 the
correction removed almost all of the gap; here a part stays, because the binomial mean is also skewed.

# 3. Which sample sizes did you investigate?

## Coarse grid, then a finer grid

My two predictions were n = `r skewN` (skewness) and n = `r gapN` (gaps), so I made the coarse grid dense from 20 to 50 and
spread out elsewhere: `r paste(pop$coarse, collapse = ", ")`. Then the code added values between the last failing and the
first passing n.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
res <- analyzePopulation(pop)
tab <- res$table
nStar <- smallestN(tab)
added <- setdiff(tab$n, pop$coarse)
showTable(tab)
```

The finer grid added `r paste(added, collapse = ", ")`.

## Which check failed?

```{r}
#| label: whichFailed
failTable <- data.frame(
  n = tab$n,
  skewOK = abs(tab$skew) <= criteria$skew,
  kurtOK = abs(tab$exKurt) <= criteria$kurt,
  qqOK = tab$qqCor >= criteria$qqCor
)
knitr::kable(failTable)
skewPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(qqCor = 0, kurt = Inf)))
qqPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(skew = Inf, kurt = Inf)))
```

Looking at each check on its own (the smallest n from which that check passed for every larger n):

* skewness: from n = `r skewPass` (prediction `r skewN`)
* QQ correlation: from n = `r qqPass` (prediction from the gaps `r gapN`)
* kurtosis passed at every n, as expected from `r round(pop$gamma2, 3)` / n.

So the skewness check passed close to its prediction, but the QQ check needed much larger n and decided the answer.

## Is it the gaps or the skewness?

The QQ correlation can be low because of the gaps or because of the skewness. As in 02die.qmd, I separated them with
two extra versions:

* Binomial with the gaps filled in: each sample mean plus a uniform random amount between −1 / (2n) and 1 / (2n).
  The gaps disappear, but the skewness stays.
* A continuous population with the same skewness: a gamma distribution with shape
  (2 / `r round(pop$gamma1, 3)`)² = `r round((2 / pop$gamma1)^2, 3)` has skewness `r round(pop$gamma1, 3)`, like the binomial, but no gaps.

```{r}
#| label: gapsOrSkew
gapGrid <- c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 100, 200)
gammaShape <- (2 / pop$gamma1)^2
gammaGen <- function(n) rgamma(n, shape = gammaShape, rate = 1)
gapsOrSkew <- do.call(rbind, lapply(gapGrid, function(n) {
  set.seed(student_id)
  binMeans <- simMeans(pop$generator, n)
  filled <- binMeans + runif(num, -1 / (2 * n), 1 / (2 * n))
  set.seed(student_id)
  gamMeans <- simMeans(gammaGen, n)
  data.frame(n = n,
             qqBinom = qqCorrelation(binMeans),
             qqFilled = qqCorrelation(filled),
             qqGamma = qqCorrelation(gamMeans),
             skewBinom = skewness(binMeans),
             skewFilled = skewness(filled),
             exKurtFilled = exKurtosis(filled))
}))
knitr::kable(gapsOrSkew, digits = 4)
filledTab <- data.frame(n = gapGrid, skew = gapsOrSkew$skewFilled,
                        exKurt = gapsOrSkew$exKurtFilled, qqCor = gapsOrSkew$qqFilled)
filledN <- smallestN(filledTab)
filledQQ <- smallestN(filledTab, modifyList(criteria, list(skew = Inf, kurt = Inf)))
gammaQQ <- smallestN(data.frame(n = gapGrid, skew = 0, exKurt = 0, qqCor = gapsOrSkew$qqGamma))
```

Without the gaps, the QQ check passed from n = `r filledQQ` (filled in binomial) and n = `r gammaQQ` (gamma), and the filled in
binomial passed all my checks from n = `r filledN`, where the skewness check decides. With the gaps, the QQ check needed
n = `r qqPass`. So the skewness of the binomial alone would give an answer near the skewness prediction; the gaps are what
pushed it up to n = `r nStar`.

## Choosing my QQ cutoff again

```{r}
#| label: qqCompare
qqValues <- c(0.995, 0.998, 0.999)
qqCompare <- data.frame(
  qqCut = qqValues,
  chosenN = sapply(qqValues, function(q) smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(qqCor = q))))
)
knitr::kable(qqCompare)
```

With 0.995 the answer is `r qqCompare$chosenN[1]` on this grid, the same as the skewness answer. With 0.998 it is `r qqCompare$chosenN[2]` and with
0.999 it is `r qqCompare$chosenN[3]`. The 0.995 value is limited by the grid, which has no n between 30 and 40; when I set
qqCor = 0.995 and reran the whole search, the finer grid gave n = 35 (see experimentLog.md), close to the skewness
prediction of `r skewN`. As on the die, the QQ cutoff decides how much discreteness I accept. I kept 0.998 for every population.

# 4. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r nStar`}$$

```{r}
#| label: summaryNumbers
star     <- tab[tab$n == nStar, ]
lastFail <- tab[tab$n == max(tab$n[tab$n < nStar & !tab$normalEnough]), ]
failed   <- c(skewness = abs(lastFail$skew) > criteria$skew,
              kurtosis = abs(lastFail$exKurt) > criteria$kurt,
              QQ = lastFail$qqCor < criteria$qqCor)
nearStar <- tab[tab$n >= 60 & tab$n <= nStar, c("n", "qqCor")]
at1      <- tab[tab$n == 1, ]
at30     <- tab[tab$n == 30, ]
seRange  <- range(tab$seRatio)
meanGapZ <- abs(tab$simMean - tab$theoMean) / (tab$theoSE / sqrt(num))
```

My predictions were n = `r skewN` from the skewness and about n = `r gapN` from the gaps; the simulation gave n = `r nStar`.
Both checks matter here, so the plot shows both.

```{r}
#| label: whyN
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4.8
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
zoom <- tab[tab$n >= 10 & tab$n <= 200, ]
nLine <- exp(seq(log(10), log(200), length.out = 300))
plot(zoom$n, zoom$skew, log = "x", pch = ifelse(zoom$normalEnough, 16, 4), lwd = 2,
     col = ifelse(zoom$normalEnough, "steelblue", "firebrick"), ylim = c(0, 0.45),
     xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "Skewness of the sample means",
     main = "Skewness passes near the prediction")
lines(nLine, pop$gamma1 / sqrt(nLine), lwd = 2)
abline(h = criteria$skew, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = c(skewN, nStar), col = c("darkorange", "steelblue"), lty = 3, lwd = 2)
legend("topright", c(paste0("Prediction ", round(pop$gamma1, 2), " / sqrt(n)"), paste("Cutoff", criteria$skew),
                     paste("Skewness prediction n =", skewN), paste("Chosen n =", nStar),
                     "Passed all checks", "Failed a check"),
       col = c("black", "firebrick", "darkorange", "steelblue", "steelblue", "firebrick"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 3, 3, NA, NA), lwd = 2, pch = c(NA, NA, NA, NA, 16, 4), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

plot(NULL, xlim = range(gapGrid), ylim = c(0.97, 1), log = "x",
     xlab = "Sample size n (log scale)", ylab = "QQ correlation",
     main = "The gaps keep the QQ correlation low")
lines(gapsOrSkew$n, gapsOrSkew$qqGamma, col = "gray50", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
lines(gapsOrSkew$n, gapsOrSkew$qqFilled, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, type = "o", pch = 16)
lines(gapsOrSkew$n, gapsOrSkew$qqBinom, col = "black", lwd = 2, type = "o", pch = 16)
abline(h = criteria$qqCor, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = nStar, col = "steelblue", lty = 3, lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("Binomial", "Binomial with gaps filled in", "Gamma, same skewness",
                        paste("Cutoff", criteria$qqCor), paste("Chosen n =", nStar)),
       col = c("black", "steelblue", "gray50", "firebrick", "steelblue"),
       lty = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3), lwd = 2, pch = c(16, 16, NA, NA, NA), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(old)
```

Left: the skewness follows the prediction `r round(pop$gamma1, 2)` / sqrt(n) and drops below my cutoff around n = `r skewN`. Right: without
the gaps (blue and gray) the QQ correlation passes my cutoff early, but the real binomial (black) only reaches it near
n = `r nStar`. The red crosses on the left between n = `r skewPass` and n = `r lastFail$n` are sample sizes where the skewness was already
fine but the QQ check failed.

# 5. How do the simulated mean and standard error compare with theory?

```{r}
#| label: seCheck
tab[, c("n", "simMean", "theoMean", "simSD", "theoSE", "seRatio", "seOK")]
```

```{r}
#| label: sePlot
plotSE(tab, label = "Binomial")
```

Center: the simulated mean was within 2 Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.5 at `r sum(meanGapZ <= 2)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes, with
a largest gap of `r round(max(meanGapZ), 2)` (at n = `r tab$n[which.max(meanGapZ)]`). Even with 24 independent checks, about 5 percent (1 or 2) would be
above 2 by chance, and these rows are not independent: they share one random stream, which is also why the mean was
below 0.5 at `r sum(tab$simMean < 0.5)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes. So I do not read this as a failure of the formula mu = 0.5.

Spread: the SE ratio stayed between `r round(seRange[1], 3)` and `r round(seRange[2], 3)`, and `r sum(tab$seOK)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes passed my
5 percent SE check, including n = 1.

# 6. Why did you choose that value?

As for the die, I set the histogram breaks halfway between the possible values of the mean (1 / n apart), so each bar
holds exactly one possible value. The red curve is the normal density with mean 0.5 and SD sigma / sqrt(n).

```{r}
#| label: samplingPlots
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 6
plotLattice(res, nShow = unique(c(1, 5, 30, nStar)), mu = pop$mu, theoSE = iidSE(pop$sigma), label = pop$label)
```

At n = 1 most of the mass is at 0 and the QQ plot is a few flat steps. At n = 5 the histogram is still clearly right
skewed and cut off at 0. At n = 30 the histogram looks roughly bell shaped, but the QQ plot still lies above the line at both ends, the
same bend that the exponential showed (a short left tail and a long right tail), and it still has visible steps. At
n = `r nStar` the bars follow the curve, the QQ plot is close to the line, and the steps are small.

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4
plotConvergence(tab, label = "Binomial")
```

The skewness follows the red prediction `r round(pop$gamma1, 2)` / sqrt(n), and the kurtosis is small at every n.

Is n = 30 enough? At n = 30 the skewness was `r round(at30$skew, 3)` (just above my cutoff), the QQ correlation was
`r round(at30$qqCor, 4)`, and the tail shares beyond ±1.96 were `r round(100 * at30$tailLow, 2)` and `r round(100 * at30$tailHigh, 2)` percent instead of 2.5 and 2.5.
So under my standard n = 30 is not enough for this population, mainly because of the gaps.

To see what this means for an actual probability, I computed the chance that the mean of 30 draws is above 0.6 (a
sum of 19 or more) in three ways: exactly from Binomial(150, 0.1), with the plain normal approximation, and with the
normal approximation evaluated half a step to the right (a sum of 18.5, a continuity correction).

```{r}
#| label: probAt30
se30 <- pop$sigma / sqrt(30)
probAt30 <- c(exact = 1 - pbinom(18, size = 150, prob = 0.1),
              normal = 1 - pnorm(0.6, mean = pop$mu, sd = se30),
              corrected = 1 - pnorm(0.6 + 1 / 60, mean = pop$mu, sd = se30))
round(probAt30, 4)
```

The plain normal approximation gives `r round(100 * probAt30["normal"], 1)` percent instead of `r round(100 * probAt30["exact"], 1)` percent, an error of
`r round(100 * (probAt30["normal"] - probAt30["exact"]), 1)` percentage points. With the correction it gives `r format(round(100 * probAt30["corrected"], 1), nsmall = 1)` percent. So at n = 30 the
plain approximation is clearly off, and most of the error comes from the gaps.

Shapiro Wilk rejected normality at `r sum(tab$swP < 0.05)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes, even where all my checks passed. As in the other files, I report
it but do not use it to decide: with 5,000 values it rejects very small departures, and a variable with gaps is very hard
for it to pass.

I chose n = `r nStar` because:

* At n = `r nStar` the skewness was `r round(star$skew, 3)`, the excess kurtosis `r round(star$exKurt, 3)` and the QQ correlation
  `r round(star$qqCor, 4)`, all within my cutoffs, and every larger n I tested also passed.
* At the largest n that still failed (n = `r lastFail$n`), the check that failed was `r paste(names(failed)[failed], collapse = " and ")`
  (QQ correlation `r round(lastFail$qqCor, 4)`).
* The gaps or skewness experiment showed that the QQ failures after the skewness passed come from the gaps.
* Near the boundary the QQ correlation rose very slowly: `r paste0(format(round(nearStar$qqCor, 5), nsmall = 5), " at n = ", nearStar$n, collapse = ", ")`. The
  cutoff is crossed in this flat part, so the exact boundary is sensitive to noise.

# 7. What surprised you?

```{r}
#| label: predictionCheck
predictionCheck <- data.frame(
  Prediction = c(
    "Mean of the sample means equals 0.5 (about 95 percent of n within 2 Monte Carlo SEs)",
    "SE equals sigma / sqrt(n) at every n, including n = 1",
    paste0("Tails 0 and about ", round(100 * sum(trueProb[3:6]), 1), " percent at n = 1"),
    paste("Skewness check passes at about n =", skewN),
    paste("Gaps decide; QQ check passes at about n =", gapN),
    "n = 30 close but not enough"
  ),
  Result = c(
    paste0("Within 2 Monte Carlo SEs at ", sum(meanGapZ <= 2), " of ", nrow(tab), " n (", round(100 * mean(meanGapZ <= 2)), "%)"),
    paste0("SE ratio ", round(seRange[1], 3), " to ", round(seRange[2], 3), "; ", sum(tab$seOK), " of ", nrow(tab), " passed"),
    paste0(round(100 * at1$tailLow, 2), "% and ", round(100 * at1$tailHigh, 2), "%"),
    paste("Skewness passed from n =", skewPass),
    paste("QQ passed from n =", qqPass, "; answer n =", nStar),
    paste0("Skewness ", round(at30$skew, 3), ", QQ ", round(at30$qqCor, 4))
  ),
  Match = c(ifelse(mean(meanGapZ <= 2) >= 0.9, "Same", "Different"), "Same", "Same",
            "Same",
            "Different", "Same")
)
knitr::kable(predictionCheck)
```

Using what I learned from the die, I predicted that the gaps would decide, and they did. But the size of the
effect surprised me: I expected about n = `r gapN` and the answer was n = `r nStar`. I had noted that the skewness could make it
larger, but not by this much. My guess assumed the binomial needs the same
step size as the die, but the binomial is also skewed, and skewness lowers the QQ correlation too (the gamma, with no
gaps at all, needed n = `r gammaQQ` for the QQ check alone). The two effects add up, so the binomial needed smaller steps than the
die.

To test this explanation, I changed p from 0.1 to 0.5 in the Console. Binomial(5, 0.5) is symmetric, so only the gaps
are left, and the same step size rule predicted n = 19. The answer was exactly n = 19 (see experimentLog.md). So
when there is no skewness the step size rule works, and the extra n for p = 0.1 comes from the skewness.

The second surprise was how different the three non normal populations are. The binomial has a smaller skewness than the
exponential (`r round(pop$gamma1, 2)` against 2), so the skewness formula says it should converge almost three times faster (n = `r skewN`
against 100). The answers were n = `r nStar` and n = 100, much closer than the formula suggests, because the binomial
pays for its gaps. The die had no skewness and small gaps and needed only n = 8. Every population failed for a
different reason, so no single rule like n = 30 fits all of them.

## Limitations

* My answer depends on the QQ cutoff: `r qqCompare$chosenN[1]` with 0.995 and `r qqCompare$chosenN[3]` with 0.999 on this grid. These two values are
  limited by the grid; a full search with 0.995 gave 35, so the 0.999 value could also be smaller than `r qqCompare$chosenN[3]`.
* My QQ check judges the normal approximation without a continuity correction. With the correction, the largest CDF gap
  at n = 30 drops from `r round(100 * exactTable$largestCdfGap[exactTable$n == 30], 1)` to `r round(100 * exactTable$withCorrection[exactTable$n == 30], 1)` percentage points, so for probability calculations with a correction a
  smaller n might be good enough.
* The boundary is uncertain: from n = `r min(nearStar$n)` to n = `r nStar` the QQ correlation changed only in the fourth decimal, so a
  different seed could move the answer by a few n.
* The gamma comparison uses a different kurtosis (`r round(6 / gammaShape, 2)` instead of `r round(pop$gamma2, 2)`), so it matches the binomial's skewness
  but not its whole shape.
* All rows come from one random stream (seed `r student_id`), so they are not independent of each other.
